descripcion_es: Which verbs are followed by -ing and which by to + infinitive: like, enjoy, want, decide…
resumen: When a verb is followed by another verb, the second one can be in -ing (enjoy reading) or in the to-infinitive (want to read). It depends on the first verb, and you have to learn it together with that verb.

filas: Try to avoid driving at night.
We can't afford to travel this year.

explicacion.texto: Like, love and hate take both forms with almost no difference: I like swimming / I like to swim. But would like, would love and would prefer always take to: I'd like to go.
After a preposition (about, of, at, in, without...) the verb always goes in -ing: I'm good at drawing; She left without saying goodbye.
Go + -ing is used for activities: go shopping, go swimming, go running.

ejemplos.frase: I enjoy walking by the sea.
Would you like to come for dinner?
Do you mind opening the window?
He's thinking of buying a flat.
ejemplos.traduccion: Está pensando en comprarse un piso.

errores_hispanohablantes.nota: Want is followed by to + infinitive.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: I'd like going to the beach.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: I'd like to go to the beach.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb (-ing or to + infinitive).
ejercicios.explicacion: Finish is in the table of verbs followed by -ing. The clue is the verb finished, just before the gap. Although Spanish says “terminar de limpiar”, with an infinitive, in English finish does not take to: the second verb goes in -ing, cleaning.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Finish does not take to + infinitive; the card puts it among the verbs that require -ing.
A calque of Spanish “terminar de”: finish is followed directly by the verb in -ing, with no preposition.
The bare infinitive cannot follow finish; you need the -ing form.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb (-ing or to + infinitive).
ejercicios.explicacion: Hope is in the table of verbs followed by to + infinitive. The clue is hope before the gap: when hope is followed directly by another verb, it always takes to. The correct form is to visit. It makes sense: hope, like want or plan, looks ahead to something that has not happened yet.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Hope is followed by to + infinitive.
ejercicios.traduccion: Esperamos visitar Escocia el próximo verano.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Hope is not used with -ing; it requires to + infinitive.
To is missing: after hope the verb goes in the to-infinitive.
It mixes the two patterns; after to comes the infinitive, visit.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb (-ing or to + infinitive).
ejercicios.frase: I'd like ___ (book) a table for two.
ejercicios.explicacion: The card stresses that would like, would love and would prefer always take to + infinitive, unlike like on its own. The clue is the contraction I'd like, which is would like. That is why, although I like cooking is correct, here only to book is possible.
ejercicios.traduccion: Querría reservar una mesa para dos.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Like takes -ing, but would like does not: it always takes to + infinitive.
To is missing: would like + to + infinitive.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb (-ing or to + infinitive).
ejercicios.frase: My grandfather stopped ___ (smoke) twenty years ago.
ejercicios.explicacion: Stop is in the table of verbs followed by -ing, with the meaning of “no longer do something”. The clue is the meaning of the sentence: the grandfather gave up the habit of smoking twenty years ago. That is why it is stopped smoking. If to smoke were used, the meaning would change: stop in order to smoke.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Stop + -ing = no longer do something (es: dejar de hacer algo).
ejercicios.traduccion: Mi abuelo dejó de fumar hace veinte años.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Stop + to means stopping in order to do something else: it would say he stopped to have a cigarette.
A calque of Spanish “dejar de”: stop is followed directly by the verb in -ing.
The bare infinitive does not follow stop; for “no longer do something” we use -ing.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete with the correct form of the verb (-ing or to + infinitive).
ejercicios.frase: She is very good at ___ (solve) problems.
ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card: after a preposition the verb always goes in -ing. The clue is good at, where at is a preposition. Although Spanish uses the infinitive (“resolver”), in English what follows a preposition must be a noun or a verb in -ing: solving.
ejercicios.traduccion: Se le da muy bien resolver problemas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The infinitive cannot follow the preposition at; you need -ing.
A preposition plus to + infinitive is not possible in English; use -ing.

ejercicios.explicacion: Promise is in the table of verbs followed by to + infinitive. The clue is promised: promising always refers to an action in the future relative to the moment of the promise, and these “future” verbs usually take to. That is why it is promised to call us.

por_opcion.calling: Incorrect: promise is not used with -ing.
por_opcion.call: Incorrect: to is missing; after promise the verb goes in the to-infinitive.

ejercicios.explicacion: Mind is among the verbs followed by -ing. The clue is the polite request Do you mind…?, which always continues with -ing: Do you mind closing the door? In Spanish we say “¿te importa cerrar?”, with an infinitive, which leads to mistakes.

por_opcion.closing: Correct: mind + -ing, also in the phrase Do you mind…?
por_opcion.to close: Incorrect: mind does not take to + infinitive.
por_opcion.close: Incorrect: the bare infinitive does not follow mind.

ejercicios.explicacion: The card includes go + -ing for activities: go shopping, go swimming, go running. The clue is go followed by the gap, with the meaning of doing a leisure activity. Neither the preposition to nor the infinitive is used: the fixed pattern is go shopping.

por_opcion.to shop: Incorrect here: go to shop would mean “go in order to buy” with a specific purpose; the activity of going shopping is go shopping.
por_opcion.shopping: Correct: go + -ing for activities, go shopping.
por_opcion.shop: Incorrect: go shop is not correct in standard English (it does appear in informal American English, but it is not the form required).

ejercicios.frase: I can't afford ___ a new car.
ejercicios.explicacion: Afford, “have enough money for something”, is followed by to + infinitive, like other verbs in the card that look ahead to a possible action (want, need, plan). The clue is can't afford. Although it is not in the table in the card, it follows the same pattern as decide or hope: can't afford to buy.
ejercicios.traduccion: No me puedo permitir comprar un coche nuevo.

por_opcion.buying: Incorrect: afford is not used with -ing.

ejercicios.explicacion: Decide is in the table of verbs followed by to + infinitive. The clue is decided: after it, the verb expressing what was decided takes to. The mistake in the sentence is using -ing, perhaps by analogy with other verbs; the correction is decided to study.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: decide does not take -ing.
To is missing: decide + to + infinitive.
After to comes the infinitive, study, not the -ing form.

ejercicios.frase: I really enjoy to travel by train.
respuestas: I really enjoy travelling by train.
I really enjoy traveling by train.
ejercicios.explicacion: Enjoy is in the table of verbs followed by -ing. The clue is enjoy, which never takes to + infinitive. Both spellings are accepted: travelling, British, with double l, and traveling, American. The natural Spanish translation is “me encanta” or “disfruto”, although English does not use like.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I really enjoy to travel by train.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: enjoy does not take to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I really enjoy travel by train.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Travel here would be a noun or a bare infinitive; after enjoy you need -ing.

ejercicios.explicacion: This applies the rule in the card: after a preposition the verb goes in -ing. Without is a preposition, so the verb that follows it cannot be in the infinitive as in Spanish (“sin decir”): without saying goodbye.

errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the sentence uncorrected: the infinitive cannot follow without.

errores_previstos.respuesta: She left without to say goodbye.
errores_previstos.explicacion: A preposition plus to + infinitive is not possible; you need -ing.

respuestas: I want to learn to drive
ejercicios.explicacion: The sentence links two verbs from the to + infinitive table: want and learn. The clue is that there are two tos among the words: one after want and another after learn. The order is subject + want + to + learn + to + drive. Notice that Spanish “aprender a” has no preposition in English, but to + infinitive.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: Want + to + infinitive; learn + to + infinitive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I want learn to to drive
errores_previstos.explicacion: Each to goes immediately before its infinitive: want to learn, learn to drive.

errores_previstos.respuesta: I to want to learn drive
errores_previstos.explicacion: To cannot go before the conjugated verb want; it goes after it.

ejercicios.explicacion: Avoid is in the table of verbs followed by -ing. The clue is avoid next to making among the words: to avoid doing something is avoid + -ing. Please can go at the beginning or at the end of an order, which is why both orders are accepted; the fixed part is avoid making noise.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The main verb of the order is avoid, and making goes after it.
The object noise goes after making, not before it (make noise, es: hacer ruido).

descripcion_larga_es: When an English verb is followed by another verb, the second one can be in -ing (enjoy reading) or in the to-infinitive (want to read), and which one is needed depends on the first verb. It is one of the most frequent sources of mistakes, because Spanish almost always uses the plain infinitive (“quiero ir”, “disfruto leyendo”). The solution is to learn each verb with its pattern.

contexto.que_es: It is the pattern a verb follows when another verb goes with it. Some verbs require -ing (enjoy, finish, mind, stop, avoid, can't stand), others to + infinitive (want, decide, hope, need, learn, would like, plan, promise) and some take both with almost no difference (like, love, hate). In addition, after any preposition the verb goes in -ing.
contexto.por_que_importa: These combinations appear in almost every sentence about likes, plans and decisions, so a mistake here is repeated constantly. Sentences like “I want go” or “I enjoy to dance” are understood, but they sound clearly foreign and in an exam they cost grammatical accuracy marks every time they appear.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: Whenever you link two verbs: talking about what you like, what you want, what you decide or what you avoid. The signal is the first verb: if it is enjoy, mind, finish or avoid, -ing; if it is want, decide, hope or would like, to. Spanish speakers tend to use the infinitive in every case and to forget to, or to use the infinitive after a preposition (“without say”).
